analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices and license generic copies if drugmakers refuse to deal.
analysis.headline: The bill had 127 Democratic cosponsors but never got a committee vote or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law forbids Medicare, the nation's largest drug buyer, from negotiating prices with pharmaceutical companies. This bill would have removed that ban and required the government to negotiate prices for drugs covered under Medicare Part D. If a drugmaker refused to negotiate a fair price, the bill would let the government license other companies to make a competing generic version of the drug — overriding the patent exclusivity the company normally holds — with 'reasonable compensation' paid to the original manufacturer. It would also cap prices during a transition period at the average price charged in ten large wealthy countries, and extend licensing to drugs bought by Medicaid, the VA, and other federal programs if the company still balked.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare's roughly 60 million beneficiaries would pay less out of pocket as negotiated prices flowed into their drug plans; the federal government and taxpayers would save on the Medicare program's drug spending; and generic manufacturers would gain new markets through competitive licenses. Seniors with no other drug coverage, and people on fixed incomes, would benefit most from lower prices on expensive brand-name drugs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the government to negotiate Medicare Part D drug prices with manufacturers, considering clinical effectiveness, patient financial burden, unmet need, and the manufacturer's global revenues and R&D investment.
If negotiation fails, the Secretary can license other companies to make the drug for Medicare despite existing patents and exclusivities, with 'reasonable compensation' to the original manufacturer.

During an interim period, prices are capped at the average charged in the ten largest OECD countries with comparable per-capita incomes, and if the manufacturer refuses, the license extends to drugs bought by Medicaid, VA, and other federal programs.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose revenues would fall as Medicare negotiated prices down and as generic competition under federal license entered markets they had locked up with patents and exclusivities.

drawbacks.text: The competitive-licensing backstop overrides patent and exclusivity protections, which drugmakers and many policymakers argue would reduce the incentive to invest in developing new medicines.
The mechanism is untested: authorizing generic production of drugs still under exclusivity would trigger years of litigation over what 'reasonable compensation' means, delaying savings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit was large: Medicare is the single biggest drug buyer, and law currently bars it from negotiating, so drug companies could charge the program above-market prices on every senior's prescriptions. The main cost is to drug-company revenue and, indirectly, to the pace of investment in new drugs: forcing licenses against manufacturers' wishes could weaken the financial incentive to develop new medicines. The bill tried to soften that by requiring "reasonable compensation" calculated from the manufacturer's R&D investment, but its enforcement teeth were strong enough that the industry would credibly oppose it. It never got an actual test, so the real-world tradeoff was never litigated or scored.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and got one subcommittee hearing, but was never voted out of committee or brought to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 1046 was introduced on February 7, 2019 with 127 Democratic cosponsors, about 55% of House Democrats.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees and to the Health Subcommittee.
The only further action in its two years was a subcommittee hearing on September 25, 2019; no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote followed before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
The bill died at the end of the 116th Congress without becoming law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drugmakers kept their legal shield against Medicare negotiation, and Medicare beneficiaries continued paying the resulting higher drug prices. The bill's main rival drug-pricing proposal passed the House that year but also stalled in the Senate.

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 7, 2019 to require Medicare drug price negotiation backed by competitive licensing.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote; the bill sat in committee for the full Congress.

against.name: Energy and Commerce Committee and Ways and Means Committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of the committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or committee vote after referral and a single subcommittee hearing.

sides.party_line_note: All 127 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and it never advanced past one subcommittee hearing.

industries.note: The bill removes their statutory protection against Medicare price negotiation and, if they refuse to deal, allows the government to license their patents and data to competitors for Medicare sales. This directly cuts the revenue they earn on the largest drug purchaser in the country.
Competitive licenses would open Medicare sales to generic producers who currently cannot enter markets protected by patents or exclusivity.
